title: Phage bet-hedging via replication slippage, and EBV antibodies
dek: Slippage is not a replication error but a phage bet: the population always carries a few individuals whose reading frame is shifted by repeats, generating variants not yet selected. Most are adapted to the current environment; when bacterial defenses escalate, the low-frequency backup takes over.
why: This episode uses two papers to present two counterintuitive mechanisms: phage variation can be a standing strategy, and effective EBV monoclonal antibodies must mature in vivo. Dense with information, suited to listeners who prefer mechanisms over conclusions.
who: R&D professionals and biotech investors working on vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, or phage therapy, who want to understand mechanisms rather than just pipeline news.

points.body: Phages do not just wait for random mutations. Their genomes contain simple sequence repeats; during DNA replication the polymerase occasionally slips, adding or deleting a base or two, shifting the reading frame and toggling a specific protein between on and off. Unlike translational frameshifting, this is a permanent change at the DNA level and is inherited by progeny. Jolene's words: making the polymerase slip here or there is much easier and faster than acquiring a new gene or repairing a broken one.

points.h: Low-level variation is a bet on the future
points.body: Bet-hedging means: most sequences fit the current environment, but a few low-frequency variants may be just right for the next one. In the bacteria-phage arms race, rather than waiting for a random mutation to be selected, slippage continuously produces low-frequency toggles. Jolene compresses the logic: you always have a low-level variant in the population that might be better suited to the next environment.

points.h: Adenine repeat length toggles defense evasion
points.body: The AGT gene itself trades off between two risks: the α-glucosyltransferase it encodes modifies phage DNA to evade the bacterial type IV restriction-modification system, but the modified DNA is then recognized by other defenses. A run of adenines in the gene comes in lengths 6, 7, or 8; different lengths shift the reading frame, turning the protein function on or off. A single slippage event lets the phage switch rapidly between two defense regimes without maintaining two gene sets.

points.h: Reversible reversion frequency is ~10,000× higher than point mutation
points.body: They chose T4's R2A gene to test this: it has a run of six adenines, and the phenotype is trackable—on hosts expressing the Rx defense system, loss of R2 function prevents plaque formation. The experiment showed that reversion mutations in this SSR region occur at a frequency about ten thousand times higher than typical point mutations. In other words, the phage can both slip to turn the gene off to evade a current defense and use the same mechanism to quickly turn it back on.

points.h: The best antibody has no in vitro shortcut
points.body: The goal was human monoclonal antibodies that neutralize EBV, but they did not rely solely on in vitro libraries like phage display; instead they returned to hybridomas: fusing B cells from immunized mice with myeloma cells, selecting with HAT medium, and screening on 384-well plates. The reason is that somatic hypermutation and junctional diversity during B cell maturation add or delete bases in CDR3, which is hard to mimic in vitro. To get a perfectly matched antibody, let B cells run the full germinal center reaction in mice, then re-express the heavy and light chain genes in cultured cells.

points.h: GP42 antibodies neutralize only B-cell infection
points.body: All eight antibodies against GP42 came from two clonal lineages; the mechanism is blocking the binding of EBV's GP42 protein to HLA class II, so they only block B-cell infection, not epithelial cells, which use a different entry mechanism. The strongest of the eight is ATX42-2. In subsequent humanized mouse experiments, 500 μg intraperitoneal injection and 11 weeks of observation, ATX42-2 prevented tumor formation, viral DNA, and splenomegaly.

points.h: Vaccine design now targets key epitopes
points.body: The GP350 subunit with alum adjuvant did not induce protective immunity, and GP42 is conformationally variable, making it hard to elicit the right antibody by conventional immunization. This paper's contribution is defining the key epitope and structural target when GP42 binds HLA class II, allowing vaccine design to work backwards. Subsequent work has seen a GP350 ferritin nanoparticle vaccine phase 1 safe and immunogenic, with seronegative participants followed to 540 days without infection; Moderna is also running an mRNA vaccine containing gHgL, GP42, and GP220.

points.h: Anti-science may be the brain saving energy
points.body: Vincent uses Kahneman's 'fast and slow' to explain anti-science: the brain defaults to low-energy System 1, while deep fact-checking is System 2, requiring extra energy and startup cost. The quote on the wall from Joshua Reynolds—'There is no expedient to which a man will not resort to avoid the real labor of thinking'—becomes the footnote to this observation. People without a statistics background hearing 'Tylenol causes autism' will have lazy System 1 accept it directly rather than seek out the literature. He stresses this is speculation, not a causal conclusion.

terms.def: Tandem repeats of short motifs in the genome; polymerase slippage during replication changes the repeat number, toggling gene function on or off.
Maintaining a minority of variants that are not adapted to the current environment but may be adapted to future ones, to cope with unpredictable change.
An immortalized cell line created by fusing an immunized B cell with a myeloma cell, capable of continuously secreting a single antibody.
A selective medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine, used to screen for successful hybridoma cells.
Mice engrafted with human hematopoietic stem cells or immune cells, used to partially reconstitute human immune processes in vivo.
